young.html: In Athens, the same festivals that showed tragedies also showed comedies, and the funniest writer of them was Aristophanes. His plays are wild fantasies: two Athenians fed up with their city persuade the birds to build a city in the clouds; a farmer flies to heaven on a giant dung beetle to bring back the goddess Peace; the god Dionysus goes down to the land of the dead to fetch back a good poet, because there are none left in Athens.

He made fun of everyone: the city's leaders, its generals, its poets, its teachers, and the audience itself. The actors wore padded costumes and masks, and the chorus dressed up as birds, wasps, clouds or frogs.

young.html: Some of his jokes are rude, the way a lot of slapstick is, so grown-ups usually choose the scenes. The Birds and The Frogs have the best family scenes: the birds building their sky city, and the chorus of frogs who croak "Brekekekex, ko-ax, ko-ax!" at Dionysus as he rows across the lake of the dead.

Write a sky city. In The Birds, the new city in the clouds is called Cloudcuckooland. Invent your own city in an impossible place (under the sea, on the Moon, inside a teapot). What is it called? Who lives there? What are its three silliest laws? Act out a visitor arriving.

full.html: Aristophanes (c. 446–c. 386 BC) wrote about 40 comedies; eleven survive, the only complete examples of the "Old Comedy" of Athens. Most were written during the Peloponnesian War, and the war, peace and the city's leaders are never far away. In The Acharnians (425 BC) a farmer makes his own private peace with Sparta. In The Knights (424 BC) he attacked the powerful politician Cleon, who, Aristophanes says, had taken him to court over an earlier play.

rows: A father sends his son to Socrates' "Thinkery" to learn to win any argument.
An old man is addicted to serving on juries.
A farmer flies a giant beetle to heaven to rescue the goddess Peace.
Two Athenians found Cloudcuckooland and cut the gods off from mankind.
Dionysus goes to the underworld to bring back a poet.
The blind god of wealth is cured, and riches go to the honest.
full.cap: Six of the eleven surviving comedies.

full.html: Sophocles and Euripides had both died in 406 BC. In The Frogs, the god of the theater, Dionysus, decides Athens needs a great poet and sets off for the underworld with his slave Xanthias, who opens the play by asking which tired old jokes he may use:

full.text: Shall I crack any of those old jokes, master, / At which the audience never fail to laugh? / Aye, what you will, except I'm getting crushed: / Fight shy of that: I'm sick of that already.
full.author: Aristophanes
full.ed: The Harvard Classics, vol. 8, P. F. Collier and Son
full.note: Two speakers: Xanthias, then Dionysus. The slashes mark line breaks.

full.html: Rowing across the lake of the dead, Dionysus is mocked by a chorus of frogs:

full.author: Aristophanes

full.note: Rogers keeps Aristophanes' Greek sound word for the croak.

full.html: In the underworld he finds Aeschylus and Euripides quarreling over the chair of best tragedian. A contest follows: the two poets quote, criticize and parody each other's verses, and finally weigh lines on a giant scale. Dionysus chooses Aeschylus, the poet of the generation that beat the Persians, to bring back to Athens. The play won first prize, and ancient sources say it was given the rare honor of a second performance because of the serious advice its chorus gave the city.

The parabasis. In the middle of an Old Comedy the actors leave and the chorus steps forward to speak straight to the audience, often for the poet himself: praise of his own plays, complaints about rivals, and advice to the city. It is a little like a comedian dropping the act.

The Clouds shows Socrates hanging in a basket to study the sky and teaching young men to make the weaker argument defeat the stronger. The real Socrates did none of this, and he later complained, in Plato's Apology (later on this ladder), that the play had helped give people a false picture of him. Plato's Symposium nonetheless shows Aristophanes and Socrates at the same dinner party, on friendly terms.
Aristophanes is our best window into everyday Athens: its law courts, markets, assembly, festivals, prices and slang. Historians use his jokes as evidence, carefully, since a joke exaggerates.
Taking the comedies as a fair report. Aristophanes was a satirist. His Socrates, his Euripides and his Cleon are cartoons, drawn for laughs, and readers have to check them against other sources.

deep.html: All eleven comedies have crude humor, and some (for example Lysistrata, about women who go on strike to end the war) build whole plots on it. Parents may want to read selections: the frog chorus, the contest of the poets in The Frogs, the founding of Cloudcuckooland in The Birds, and the rescue of Peace.

Old Comedy could name and mock living, powerful people in front of thousands of citizens. Ancient writers already disagreed about how free it was: some reported attempts to limit mockery by name, and Aristophanes says he was prosecuted by Cleon. After Athens lost the war, comedy turned toward plots about ordinary families; the "New Comedy" of Menander, a century later, is the ancestor of the Roman comedy of Plautus and Terence and, through them, of modern situation comedy.

items: Can a joke be unfair? Is it different when the target is powerful?
Why might laughing at a city's leaders be good for the city? Can it also do harm?
In The Frogs, a comedy argues about what makes a great tragedy. Can comedy be serious?
Was it fair of Aristophanes to put a real person, Socrates, on stage as a fraud?

questions: Aristophanes invented a city in the clouds. If you could found a new city, what would its laws be?
Why do people enjoy jokes about famous or powerful people? Where is the line between fun and unkind?
The frogs keep croaking to annoy Dionysus. What is the most annoying sound you know, and how would you put it in a play?
Socrates said the comedy gave people the wrong idea about him. Can a funny story spread a false picture? Can you think of an example?
In The Frogs, Dionysus chooses the older poet. Do you think old books or new books have more to teach?
care: Ancient comedy has a lot of crude humor. This lesson quotes and summarizes only family-suitable parts. The Birds (the sky city) and The Frogs (the frog chorus and the contest of poets) have the best scenes for families, read in selections.
